draft.title: Changing evidence about the past
card: Historians write about the past using evidence, such as burials, tools and dating tests. New evidence can change what they know.
Ancient burials at Lake Mungo in New South Wales showed that people lived in Australia tens of thousands of years ago.
Dating at Madjedbebe, in the Northern Territory, pushed the known age of human life in Australia back even further.
Each new find means historians revise their accounts. They write about the past with the best evidence they have, and they change it when better evidence appears.
draft.remember: New finds can push back dates, so historians update their accounts.

a.q: Why have historians changed their writing about when people first lived in Australia?
opts: New finds and dating gave older evidence of human life
Older books were lost, so the dates had to be guessed
People moved to Australia later than first thought
Historians prefer to change their accounts every few years
a.why: Finds such as Lake Mungo and dating at Madjedbebe gave older evidence, so accounts were revised. The option about later arrival is wrong because the evidence pushed the dates back, not forward.
a.clue: Think about what the new evidence showed.

b.q: A museum guide says, "Our display about early life in Australia was rewritten after a new dating result." What does this show about history?
opts: Accounts of the past can change when new evidence appears
Earlier historians were careless, so their work is useless
The past itself changed when the dating result came out
Dating results are always final and can never be revised
b.why: Historians revise accounts when better evidence arrives. The past did not change; only what we know about it did.
b.clue: What changed: the past, or what historians know?

a.best: New finds and dating gave older evidence of human life

b.best: Accounts of the past can change when new evidence appears
